Dear Reviewers,

The ending of the discussion period is only a few days away. We would be obliged if you considered our responses and updates to the manuscript.

Thank you,
Authors

> Can the authors include FLOP or runtime comparisons beyond parameter count?

Tables 4 and 7 show runtime comparisons for the GPT2-xl and Llama-3.2B models. As can be seen our models are much faster to train and infer. For training GPT2-xl models, we are faster by 12hrs on OWT and 26hrs on GW. For the bigger Llama models (3.2B size) whose results we now report in Tables 6 and 7, our throughput is much higher with training being faster by 2 days. We thus envision that these speedups will be even more acute for larger models. Inference gains shown in Table 4 are also significant given that these are per sample inference times and when you consider the sizes of the datasets are in the billions (viz. OWT, GW) or even trillions of tokens (now with docling dataset for Llama), this can lead to 10s of hours in inference time savings when using the trained model to infer on these datasets.

> What is the exact computational complexity of CoFr attention?

Both variants in Figure 2 have linear complexity as there is no matrix-matrix multiplication (viz. QK) required to obtain attention weights as is the case with standard attention. The left architecture in Figure 2 directly weighs the previous tokens based on the upper triangular linear layer ($O(lp)$ complexity) and the right architecture creates attention weights just as a function of the current token (again $O(lp)$ complexity) without referring to each of the individual previous tokens.

> Would including concise pseudocode or an algorithm outline improve readability?

Thanks for the suggestion. However, we weren’t certain what exactly to add as the forward and backward passes simply follow Figure 4 for the CoFrNet components that are replaced in the model architectures. If there are any specific suggestions you have we would be glad to execute them.

> How does the model handle (long-context) reasoning?

In our new experiments in Table 6, where we replace components of a Llama-3.2B model pre-trained on the docling data mix with 2T tokens (see lines 379-383), we report performance on eight different tasks, including open domain Q\&A, reasoning and text understanding. As can be seen, we observe qualitatively similar behavior for the Llama models as we saw with GPT2 even when tested on these diverse tasks, where CoFrGeNet-F is the best on majority of these tasks, while the other variants are still competitive with the original Llama model.

> Are there training curves showing convergence and stability trends?

In Figure 13 in the appendix we now show the training curves for the different variants on OWT. As can be seen the training is quite stable. The training was stable on GW and docling as well. However, since the runs had to be restarted multiple times from intermediate checkpoints due to hardware errors (GPUs fail sometimes given the duration of the runs for reasons not in our control), we were unable to obtain a single plot directly tracing the whole training. We will however, create those for the final version.

summary.value: The paper proposes a new architecture that replaces attention and feed-forward layers in Transformers with continued fraction-based modules. This design reduces parameter count and computational cost while achieving competitive performance to GPT2-xl and efficient-attention baselines on GLUE and perplexity evaluations. The authors also demonstrate training and inference speed improvements, particularly when leveraging their “continuants” formulation for gradient computation.

strengths.value:
1. Introduces an original mathematical formulation (continued fractions) to model dependencies, offering a new theoretical direction beyond attention.

2. Demonstrates reasonable empirical results, outperforming baselines while using fewer parameters.

3. Provides clear efficiency gains in both training and inference, showing practical relevance for language modeling.

weaknesses.value:
1. My main concern lies in the evaluation scope of the proposed model. While the continued fraction-based architecture might be new and shows encouraging results, the experiments are limited to GPT2-scale models and GLUE benchmarks. This restricted evaluation leaves open questions about the model’s scalability, robustness, and generalization to more complex or diverse settings such as larger models or broader benchmarks such as reasoning and long-context tasks. A more comprehensive evaluation would strengthen the paper’s claims about efficiency and performance across different architectures and data regimes.

2. The method’s implementation complexity and generalization to other architectures (e.g., MoE or diffusion-based) remain unexplored.

questions.value: How does the model perform on larger-scale models and broader benchmarks?

comment.value: We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. We are glad that **novelty**, **ease of use** being a plug-in replacement and **parameter efficiency** of our architectures were appreciated. We respond below to the specific concerns of the reviewers noting that we have **uploaded an updated version of the paper** addressing the major concerns.

> effect of the training schedule

Table 5 in the updated paper shows the impact of our training schedule. Without the schedule the perplexities are significantly worse.

> Table 4 shows that the best CoFreGeNet is only about 20 microseconds better than the gpt-2xl inference time

The 20 microseconds gain is **per sample**. This is significant when you consider that the sizes of the datasets are in the billions (viz. OWT, GW) or even trillions of tokens (now with the docling dataset for Llama), which can lead to 10s of hours in inference time savings, when using the trained model to infer on these datasets. Moreover, the training time is also much less, where for the GPT2-xl models we are faster by 12hrs on OWT and 26hrs on GW. For the bigger Llama models (3.2B size) whose results we now report in Tables 6 and 7, our throughput is much higher with training being faster by 2 days. We thus envision that these speedups will be even more acute for larger models.

> unclear where the latency improvements come from

Although the projection step is retained (as you wrote), the number of matrix multiplications (as well as parameters) is much fewer for us which leads to speed ups. For example, for attention we do not have to do the expensive QK (i.e. $p\times p$ matrix) multiplications seen in standard attention. For feedforward, every layer of an MLP adds quadratic complexity, while for us every layer has linear complexity since a single parameter vector is multiplied with the input ($O(p)$ time) and not a $\alpha p\times p$ matrix, where $\alpha>>1$ is the expansion factor in the MLPs.

> not very evident that the method gives consistent accuracy improvements with greater efficiency

We would like to note that our goal is to propose architectural options which lead to competitive models with the current transformer models but with fewer parameters. Surpassing performance (viz. accuracy) is not our expectation given that we are parameter efficient. Given the novelty of the function class and architectures, we believe that even being in the ballpark in terms of performance is a meaningful contribution, since the community can further improve upon these ideas. The fact that we surpassed transformer models in some cases speaks to the potential of these architectures, but should not necessarily be an expectation. Please also note that the current maturity of transformer architectures (originally published in 2017) is a result of years of work by thousands of people. It would be exciting to see where similar effort put into our proposed architectures would lead to. 

Additionally, to put things into perspective, in a recent NeurIPS paper [1] adapting Diffusion models for language generation, the authors also pre-trained their model on OWT (and one other dataset), results were also reported on GLUE, and the size of the models was only on the 100M parameter scale. This is much smaller than what we have tested for our new architectures. Nevertheless, this paper has almost 300 citations and has had significant impact.

The bigger variants performing better is hence expected, and even with just replacing feedforward layers (i.e. CoFrGeNet-F variant), the size of the models is $\approx \frac{2}{3}$ of the original which is significant savings in practical terms. Moreover, current hardware is not optimized to our architectures as they are new, and hence hardware innovation — which is part of our future efforts — is likely to further speed up our models. We hope you consider these aspects and the future potential of these architectures as they evolve.

> Can you provide any other metrics that improve while using your custom gradient change the optimization landscape (stability) ?

Our custom gradient (continuant-based) computation is primarily for speedup in training and inference. It does not change the optimization landscape by much (slight practical change because of fewer poles to consider) as the continuant formalism is equivalent to optimizing layerwise. The main benefit is it reduces the number of divisions from $d$ to $1$ for a $d$-depth ladder, where divisions are known to be significantly more expensive than multiplications or additions on modern hardware. As seen in Table 4, this impact is significant where we save 10s of hours in training time (CoFrGeNet vs CoFrGeNet$_B$) and are almost an order of magnitude faster in inference even on a single sample.

> Table 2 and Table 3 hinder natural reading

We have reformatted the text around the tables to make reading easier per your suggestion.

1] S. S. Sahoo, M. Arriola, A. Gokaslan, E. M. Marroquin, A. M. Rush, Y. Schiff, J. T. Chiu, and V. Kuleshov. Simple and effective masked diffusion language models. NeurIPS 2024.

summary.value: This paper introduces CoFrGeNet, a new architecture for language generation based on continued fractions. The authors replace Transformer attention and FFN layers with CoFrNet modules, using a continuant-based gradient formulation to reduce division operations and improve efficiency. Models are pretrained on OpenWebText and GneissWeb and show comparable or better results than GPT-2-xl on GLUE and language modeling tasks, while using fewer parameters and less training time.

strengths.value:
- Novel and mathematically grounded idea — continued fractions as neural components.
- Clear derivations and theory with interpretable structure.
- Plug-and-play replacement for Transformer layers; minimal training changes needed.
- Custom gradient and training schedule improve efficiency and stability.

weaknesses.value:
- No analysis of compute cost or FLOPs; efficiency claims incomplete.
- Attention complexity (Figure 2) not analyzed with respect to sequence length.
- Pseudocode or in-paper algorithmic overview would improve clarity, even though code is provided separately.
- Limited scaling experiments; unclear behavior for larger models.
- No long-context or “needle-in-a-haystack” tests to verify causal mixing.

> How does the model perform on larger-scale models and broader benchmarks?

As you must know, pre-training is significantly more expensive than fine-tuning and hence pre-training very large models in the rebuttal period is hard. Nonetheless, in the updated manuscript we now report results on Llama 3.2B pre-trained on the docling data mix, which is a mixture of nine different datasets consisting of web, multilingual, math, code and synthetic data (see lines 379-383) and is heavily used to train models for document understanding. We trained on a recommended 2T size sample. For evaluation, we tested our pre-trained models on eight different tasks covering open domain Q&A, reasoning and text understanding. These results are shown in Table 6. As can be seen, we observe qualitatively similar behavior for the Llama models as we saw with GPT2 even when tested on these diverse tasks, where CoFrGeNet-F is the best on majority of these tasks, while the other variants are still competitive with the original Llama model. The throughputs are observed in Table 7. We see that our variants are faster than the original Llama, where CoFrGeNet-F and CoFrGeNet take as much as a couple of days less to train.

Also to put things into perspective a bit, in a recent NeurIPS paper [1] adapting Diffusion models for language generation, the authors also pre-trained their model on OWT (and one other dataset), results were also reported on GLUE, and the size of the models was only on the 100M parameter scale. This is much smaller than what we have tested for our new architectures. Nevertheless, this paper has almost 300 citations and has had significant impact. We hope this aspect is considered in your assessment.

> method’s implementation complexity and generalization to other architectures

Now that we have applied our method to Llama which has a very different architecture than GPT2, we hope this concern is alleviated. As such, Llama uses Grouped Query Attention (GQA) as opposed to standard (Flash) attention in GPT2 and uses gated feedforward layers as opposed to a vanilla multilayer perceptron. Experimentation with MOE architectures we leave as future work, as we stated in the paper. We believe however, that our architectures should almost seamlessly apply as the multiple experts, which are simply multiple (vanilla) feedforward layers, should each be replaceable by our CoFrNet replacement for feedforward (i.e. architecture in Figure 3). The attention mechanisms, which are a combination of GQA and sliding window in many cases, should also be replaceable by our attention replacements in Figure 2.

1] S. S. Sahoo, M. Arriola, A. Gokaslan, E. M. Marroquin, A. M. Rush, Y. Schiff, J. T. Chiu, and V. Kuleshov. Simple and effective masked diffusion language models. NeurIPS 2024.

summary.value: This work proposes replacing the transformer attention and feed-forward (FFN) layers with faster components that are inspired by continued fractions. Since their formulations utilizes division-operations which are slower - they design a custom gradient formulation that reduces divisions during training (from d divisions to 1). They compare their models trained with the ladder with GPT-2-XL on perplexity and GLUE tasks and show competitive performance using fewer parameters.

strengths.value: The paper does seem to show that the ladder-fused models get competitive performance with fewer parameters. The ladder-setup also seems easy to plug into existing architectures.

weaknesses.value:
- Latency argument needs more support - Since the final architecture for the proposed method retains the projection step and uses affine transformations - it seems like a large amount of compute is still allocated to matmul operations. Only the internal non-linearity is replaced by the optimized division introduced by the authors; It’s unclear if this is enough to claim the latency improvements (which aren’t empirically very clear as well as Table 4 shows that the best CoFreGeNet is only about 20 microseconds better than the gpt-2xl inference time ?). 

- Accuracy-Parameter efficiency trends are irregular - For Table-3, the biggest variants show the most competitive performance where the parameter efficiency isn’t as substantial. A few tasks show competitive performance at best (when Standard deviation is taken into consideration) so it’s not very evident that the method gives consistent accuracy improvements with greater efficiency. 

- Some ablations would make the stability of the method more evident: Some decisions in the paper are not very well justified right now - for instance, the effect of the training schedule adopted by the authors. Including that will make the claims more stable. 

Comment (not a weakness): Consider placing text around the wrap tables as Table 2 and Table 3 hinder natural reading significantly.

summary.value:
The paper proposes continued-fraction–based replacements for Transformer attention and FFN layers, motivated by parameter efficiency and potential runtime benefits. Reviewers acknowledge the originality of the mathematical formulation and the plug-in nature of the components, as well as some empirical competitiveness at smaller scales.

However, several core concerns remain unresolved. The empirical evaluation, while extended in the rebuttal, still lacks targeted long-context or robustness tests, leaving scalability claims insufficiently substantiated. Efficiency claims rely mainly on wall-clock runtime comparisons without clear FLOP-level or hardware-normalized analysis, making it difficult to isolate architectural contributions from training schedules, implementation choices, or data effects. Generalization beyond standard Transformer variants is largely speculative.

Reviewer opinions are mixed, with marginal scores on both sides and explicit statements indicating comfort with a negative outcome. No reviewer provided an explicit post-rebuttal signal indicating resolved major concerns or a score increase.

Given the interrupted process, this assessment reflects a best-effort, conservative judgment based solely on the available reviews, rebuttal, and limited discussion, without assuming any unexpressed score changes.
